r1-handoff.finding:
FAIL, BLOCKING on the negative-test-teeth finding (the handoff's Q4, the sharpest one). All
four of the handoff's named questions graded below, then the "Also verify" items.

=== Q4: Do the negative tests have teeth? CONFIRMED VACUOUS, BLOCKING ===

Ran the exact attack the handoff prescribed: disabled flag emission on ONE code path in
extract.run() -- added `stale = []` immediately after the real `stale = sorted(...)` computation
(scripts/code_map/extract.py, inside run()'s `with open(outp, "w"...) as f:` block) -- then reran
the closing selector `python -m pytest tests/test_code_map.py -k 'stale_tag' -q --color=no`.

Baseline (unmutated): 12 passed. Mutated (emission disabled): 9 passed, 3 failed, exactly matching
an a-priori prediction made before running. Reverted the mutation immediately after
(`git status --porcelain -- scripts/code_map/extract.py` clean; reran the selector: 12 passed
again, confirming a clean restore).

The 3 that went red are the only ones with real teeth against this attack:
  StaleAnchorExtractionTests.test_stale_tag_flags_a_real_body_change_across_two_extractions
  StaleAnchorRenderReportTests.test_stale_tag_render_report_flags_a_real_body_change
  StaleAnchorRenderReportTests.test_stale_tag_render_report_carries_no_timing_field (red only
    incidentally, via its own "input precondition" assertion that a flag actually landed --
    the timing-field scan itself never ran)

The 9 that stayed GREEN under total feature disablement include EVERY dedicated "does not flag"
test in the suite:
  test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_nothing
  test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_a_reformat_across_two_extractions
  test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_an_unrelated_anchor
  test_stale_tag_render_report_does_not_flag_a_reformat
  test_stale_tag_render_report_does_not_fail_the_build (trivially true when nothing is ever
    flagged, so of course the exit code stays 0)
  test_stale_tag_span_hash_is_persisted_on_every_anchored_statement (checks a different property,
    correctly orthogonal to this attack)
  SpanHashUnitTests' three tests (hash-unchanged-by-reformat, hash-unchanged-by-docstring-edit,
    hash-changes-on-real-change) -- these call span_hash() directly, a genuinely different, lower
    unit than run()'s diffing, correctly untouched by an attack on run()'s emission path, and NOT
    vacuous on their own terms: test_stale_tag_hash_changes_on_a_real_body_change already gives
    them their own internal positive control (h1 != h2 on a real mutation), so these three are
    fine as written.

This is exactly the shape the handoff named ("the same defect class as this run's tc38 and tc47")
and exactly the threshold the handoff pre-declared as BLOCK-worthy ("if most of the negatives stay
green ... that is a BLOCK-worthy finding even though the feature works"). 6 of the 9 EXTRACTION-
and RENDER-level tests in this gate's own two headline test classes (StaleAnchorExtractionTests,
StaleAnchorRenderReportTests) -- everything except the two "flags a real change" tests and the
persisted-hash test -- would not catch a regression that silently disabled staleness detection
entirely. A future refactor that accidentally comments out or short-circuits the `stale =
sorted(...)` line (or any equivalent full-disable) ships green.

The feature ITSELF genuinely works -- the two "flags" tests have real teeth (confirmed: they are
exactly what went red) -- so this is not a claim the capability is broken. It is a claim that most
of the shipped regression guard cannot fail, which CREW_CONTEXT.md's verification-discipline
section lists first among the rules that most often separate an accepted change from a reworked
one here ("A check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passed").

RULING: BLOCKING. Fix shape: give each "does not flag" test its own positive control in the SAME
test method (assert a known-should-flag mutation DOES flag, in the same test that asserts the
target case does not) -- e.g. test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_an_unrelated_anchor already builds the
fixture where widget-spin SHOULD be stale; it should also assert "widget-spin" IS in
_stale_slugs(after) in the SAME method it asserts "holder-hold" is not, so a full-disable
regression cannot leave it green. Same shape applies to test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_
nothing (add a second extraction in the same test that DOES flag) and to the two render-report
"does not flag" tests.

=== Q1: Does slug-match beg the question? CORRECTLY-DEFERRED G7 CONCERN, not a defect now ===

Confirmed directly: grepped scripts/code_map/ for comment-tag vocabulary (Assumption:/
Constraint:/etc.) -- zero hits, and the real repo's own fresh render_report.json (built this
review, see below) shows "ids": 0, zero anchors anywhere in this corpus today. The ONLY authored-
identity surface that exists pre-g7 is the [slug] anchor itself, so matching old-vs-new by slug
IS the only "same tag" test available today -- the crew's reasoning holds as stated.

Going further than the crew's own writeup: this mechanism tracks the CODE's hash only, never a
tag's own prose (which does not exist yet). Once g7 lands, this has a real, permanent consequence
that is NOT a bug g7 will "fix" by widening the hook -- it is baked into what span_hash measures:
the flag fires on ANY code change under a live tag, EVEN ONE where the human already updated the
tag's prose correctly in the same commit. There is no way for this mechanism, as built, to
distinguish "prose is now stale" from "prose was already fixed, but the code changed too." That
is consistent with the crew's own accepted-cost stance on the local-variable-rename blind spot
(over-flag, never under-flag, is the accepted direction of error) -- see the Decision-anchor
ruling below -- so I read this as the SAME accepted direction of error, not a new problem, but it
should be named explicitly as a permanent design property for g7 to inherit, not something g7's
build will make go away.

RULING: correctly-deferred g7 concern. No rework required now.

=== Q2: Is advisory-only right, and does the FAIL text collide? COLLISION CONFIRMED, real finding ===

Confirmed by reading checks.py directly: checks.run() (the `check` subcommand) prints REAL,
build-relevant failures as `FAIL {name}: {count}` (scripts/code_map/checks.py:833) -- the exact
same "FAIL " prefix convention render.py's new advisory line uses: `FAIL stale tag [%s]: ...`
(render.py:721). render.py ALSO already used this convention for an unambiguous, build-failing
condition: `FAIL duplicate id [%s] claimed by: %s` (render.py:713), which DOES fail the build
(`return 1 if duplicates else 0`, render.py:730) -- while the new stale-tag line, by design, never
affects the return code.

Traced the call graph via cli.py: `build` runs extract.run() then render.run() (cli.py's
_build) -- so a SINGLE `build` invocation's own stdout can legally contain BOTH "FAIL duplicate
id [...]" (build-failing) and "FAIL stale tag [...]" (advisory only) side by side, distinguishable
ONLY by exit code, never by the printed text. `check` is a SEPARATE subcommand (checks.py's own
run(), never calls render.py) -- so the two conventions never appear in the SAME command's stdout,
but they DO appear in the same combined transcript for the gate's own documented standard
procedure ("Fresh build then check (in that order)"): a human or script reading that transcript
end to end sees three different "FAIL "-prefixed line shapes across the two commands, two of which
are build-failing and one of which is not.

This is exactly what the handoff asked me to check for, and it is real: "whether anything (a
script, a CI grep, a human skimming) could reasonably read FAIL and conclude the build failed."
Yes -- the SAME prefix a real check failure already uses, in the SAME command's own output, in the
gate's own standard-procedure transcript.

Severity: I agree advisory-only is the right SEVERITY given this repo's own inherited stance (a
stale tag is not unambiguous corruption the way a duplicate id is; failing the build on it would
train people to ignore a real signal, matching the code's own "gb's ruling" comment -- I checked
this citation and could not find gb's OWN gate producing a literal ruling about build-failing vs
advisory severity specifically; gb's actual scope is the four ratio-based thresholds. The
"twitchy tripwire" language traces to this gate's own Commander plan
(g6-implementer-plan.json:185), not a verbatim gb decision. Not a blocker on its own -- the
REASONING is sound and consistent with gb's own documented philosophy of avoiding twitchy
absolute-count invariants -- but the citation is looser than "the gb ruling" implies; worth a
lighter phrasing next time ("in the spirit of gb's ratio-over-count philosophy") rather than
citing it as a specific ruling.

RULING on severity: advisory-only stands. RULING on the text collision: real, should-fix, not on
its own blocking (Q4 is what blocks this gate), but should be fixed in the same rework pass --
change the advisory line's prefix to something that cannot be mistaken for a build-failing check
(e.g. "ADVISORY stale tag [...]" or "WARN stale tag [...]"), a one-line fix.

=== Q3: Attack reformatting immunity with novel mutations -- ALL PREDICTIONS CONFIRMED, no new defect ===

Wrote a standalone attack script calling extract.span_hash() directly on 8 paired snippets NOT
in the crew's own probe set (quote-style change, backslash line continuation, paren-wrapped
multi-line, changed default-argument value, reordered independent statements, added a type
annotation, integer-literal-to-equivalent-expression, for-loop-to-comprehension), predicting
flag/no-flag BEFORE running each. Result: 8/8 predictions matched exactly.

No-flag confirmed (all three lexical-only changes): quote-style, backslash-continuation,
paren-wrap -- consistent with ast.dump encoding the Constant VALUE and node structure only, never
source text/whitespace (include_attributes=False, as the docstring already states).

Flag confirmed (all four AST-structural changes, even where runtime BEHAVIOR is unchanged):
default-arg-value, statement-reorder (ast.dump encodes body-list order), add-type-annotation
(a new AST node), int-literal-to-equivalent-expression (Constant(2) vs BinOp(1+1) differ in AST
though the runtime value is identical), for-loop-to-comprehension (very different AST shapes for
equivalent behavior).

Every result follows directly and only from ast.dump's documented behavior -- nothing accidental,
nothing that contradicts the crew's own stated mechanism. The syntactic-but-behaviorally-inert
false-positive cases (literal-to-equivalent-expression, reordering, annotations) are the SAME
accepted "over-flag, never under-flag" direction of error already named for the local-variable-
rename blind spot -- not a new defect class, but worth naming precisely: the immunity claim holds
EXACTLY as claimed (reformatting/comments/docstrings), and nothing more.

RULING: no defect. Confirms the crew's own claim precisely, with 8 novel mutations, no accidental
behavior found.

=== "Also verify" items ===

1. deterministic-rebuild structurally cannot exercise the staleness path -- CONFIRMED by direct
   code read, not accepted on the crew's word: checks.py's _build_into() (checks.py:730) builds
   into a FRESH tempfile.mkdtemp() workdir/artifacts path on EVERY call, and deterministic_rebuild
   (checks.py:778) calls it twice into TWO separate fresh scratch dirs (workdir/a, workdir/b).
   os.path.exists(outp) is False both times, so old_hashes = {} both times -- the staleness branch
   in extract.run() never executes inside this check. Corollary confirmed and it DOES bother me
   somewhat, though it is not this gate's defect to fix: `check` (the subcommand a Commander is
   told to run second, per this gate's own close criteria) NEVER exercises the staleness path at
   all, by construction -- only `build` run twice into the SAME `--artifacts` dir does (a local,
   iterative-development usage pattern). Given `.code-map`/`map` are gitignored (confirmed via
   `git check-ignore -v .code-map` -- statements.jsonl/extract_report.json/render_report.json are
   all ignored) and no `.github/workflows/*.yml` references code_map at all (grepped -- zero
   hits), this mechanism's only routine exerciser today is a human/agent iterating locally without
   wiping .code-map between builds, e.g. exactly this project's own gate-to-gate Commander/
   reviewer workflow (each gate's close criteria run `build` into the SAME default `--artifacts`
   path relative to `--root`, gate after gate) -- once real anchors exist. Flagging as an
   observation, not a blocker: the mechanism's only exerciser is an unenforced convention (don't
   wipe `.code-map` between runs), not a checked invariant.

2. Read-before-overwrite robustness -- REPRODUCED A REAL CRASH, not previously reported.
   - First-ever run (no previous statements.jsonl): confirmed safe by the shipped
     test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_nothing (os.path.exists(outp) False -> old_hashes={}).
   - Slug newly added or removed between runs: confirmed safe by direct code read -- a new slug is
     only in new_hashes (never compared, no flag, no crash); a removed slug is only in old_hashes
     (the loop iterates new_hashes.items(), never visits it) -- matches the code's own comment
     ("this gate's concern... see DESIGN_SPEC's Tombstones section").
   - Truncated / malformed previous statements.jsonl: REPRODUCED A CRASH. Built a real fixture
     repo, ran `extract` once (succeeds), truncated the last line of the resulting
     statements.jsonl mid-JSON (simulating an interrupted prior run -- a real scenario, since
     extract.run()'s OWN writer is a plain `with open(outp, "w")` with no atomic rename, so a
     killed process leaves exactly this kind of partial last line), then ran `extract` again
     against the same --artifacts dir. Result: uncaught `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Invalid
     control character...`, propagating all the way out, exit code 1, with a bare Python
     traceback naming no file path and no actionable next step. This is a NEW failure mode this
     gate introduces: before g6, extract.run() never read the old store, so a corrupted leftover
     statements.jsonl from an earlier interrupted run was harmless (the next run would just
     overwrite it and succeed). Now a corrupted leftover store makes EVERY subsequent extraction
     fail outright until a human manually deletes the file, and the traceback gives no hint that
     THIS is the fix. Not tested anywhere in the shipped suite (grepped
     StaleAnchorExtractionTests/StaleAnchorRenderReportTests -- no malformed-store test exists).
     RULING: real robustness regression, should-fix (wrap the old-hash read in a try/except that
     treats an unreadable store as absent, printing a named warning, mirroring "fail visibly"
     doctrine -- crashing IS visible, but with no actionable message and a NEW failure mode where
     none existed before). Contributes to, but does not by itself drive, the BLOCK verdict (Q4
     already drives it).

3. Count discrepancy -- CONFIRMED: "12" is right, "16" in the RESULT's Scope section is simply
   wrong. Counted directly from the diff: StaleAnchorExtractionTests (5 methods) +
   StaleAnchorRenderReportTests (4 methods) + SpanHashUnitTests (3 methods) = 12, matching the
   Evidence section and my own independent test run (12 passed, both before and after my
   revert). Nothing was dropped between writing and shipping -- this is a drafting error confined
   to the RESULT document's Scope section, not a shipped-behavior defect.

4. extract_report.json's secondary stale_tags field -- judged: harmless duplication on the
   BLESSED `build` path (extract then render in one process, same statements.jsonl round-tripped
   immediately), because both reports derive from the identical `stale` list computed once inside
   extract.run() -- extract_report.json writes `stale` directly; render_report.json re-derives
   the same slugs by reading the very statements.jsonl rows that same `stale` list just produced.
   They cannot diverge within one `build` invocation. BUT the CLI supports invoking `extract` and
   `render` as independently-timed stages (cli.py's own STAGES tuple), and if a human runs `render`
   alone against a `statements.jsonl` from an OLDER `extract` run than the one that produced the
   currently-cached `extract_report.json`, the two reports WOULD read as different snapshots of
   different runs. This is not new to this gate -- extract_report.json's existing `failures` field
   carries the identical latent risk today, pre-dating g6 -- so I do not treat this as a g6-
   specific defect, just as an observation worth naming since the handoff asked directly. Filed as
   a triage candidate below (tc1), not a blocker.

All REPRODUCIBLE evidence in IMPLEMENTER_RESULT reproduced exactly, independently, this run: full
suite 1805 passed / 2 skipped / 683 subtests / 0 failed / exit 0 (384.94s); fresh build+check
7/7 exit 0 with deterministic-rebuild included; closing selector -k 'stale_tag' 12
collected/12 passed/exit 0; render_report.json on a fresh build carries stale_tags: [] and

The DEMONSTRATES-THE-BEHAVIOR question is where this splits:

- The POSITIVE capability (the mechanism CAN detect a real staleness event) is genuinely
  demonstrated and, this review, genuinely attacked: 8 novel reformatting-immunity mutations (Q3)
  all matched a-priori predictions, and the "flags a real change" tests are exactly what went red
  under the whole-feature-disable attack (Q4) -- real teeth, not decoration.

- The NEGATIVE evidence -- the 6 "does not flag" tests offered as proof the mechanism correctly
  discriminates a harmless edit from a real one -- does NOT demonstrate what it is offered to
  demonstrate. Disabling emission on one code path in extract.run() (stale = [] forced after the
  real computation) leaves 9 of 12 tests green, including EVERY dedicated "does not flag" test.
  As independent regression evidence, most of this suite cannot distinguish "the mechanism
  correctly said nothing" from "the mechanism was never wired up at all." Full detail, the exact
  attack, and the fix shape are recorded under r1-handoff -- not repeated here.

This is precisely the CREW_CONTEXT.md verification-discipline rule listed first among those most
often separating an accepted change from a reworked one in this repo: "A check that cannot fail is
indistinguishable from one that passed. Before you offer a check as evidence, demonstrate it can
reach a failing state." Most of this gate's own negative evidence was never demonstrated reaching
a failing state against the actual regression it is meant to guard (the whole detector silently
going dark), only against the ONE probe the crew itself chose (deleting a `sorted()` call, an
unrelated function to this feature) -- these tests were not attacked with the feature's own
disablement before being offered as evidence.

RULING: FAIL here for the same reason r1-handoff fails -- the shipped CAPABILITY works (confirmed
independently, twice, under attack), but the evidence document's own negative tests do not carry
the weight IMPLEMENTER_RESULT implicitly assigns them ("Reformatting-immunity demonstration"
section cites two of these six tests as its proof). Not a rework of what ships to a REAL repo with
real anchors -- Q4's ruling under r1-handoff already covers the fix. Filed jointly with r1-handoff,
same triage/rework item, not a second independent blocker.

findings:
r1-handoff: FAIL, BLOCKING on the negative-test-teeth finding (the handoff's Q4, the sharpest one). All
four of the handoff's named questions graded below, then the "Also verify" items.

=== Q4: Do the negative tests have teeth? CONFIRMED VACUOUS, BLOCKING ===

Ran the exact attack the handoff prescribed: disabled flag emission on ONE code path in
extract.run() -- added `stale = []` immediately after the real `stale = sorted(...)` computation
(scripts/code_map/extract.py, inside run()'s `with open(outp, "w"...) as f:` block) -- then reran
the closing selector `python -m pytest tests/test_code_map.py -k 'stale_tag' -q --color=no`.

Baseline (unmutated): 12 passed. Mutated (emission disabled): 9 passed, 3 failed, exactly matching
an a-priori prediction made before running. Reverted the mutation immediately after
(`git status --porcelain -- scripts/code_map/extract.py` clean; reran the selector: 12 passed
again, confirming a clean restore).

The 3 that went red are the only ones with real teeth against this attack:
  StaleAnchorExtractionTests.test_stale_tag_flags_a_real_body_change_across_two_extractions
  StaleAnchorRenderReportTests.test_stale_tag_render_report_flags_a_real_body_change
  StaleAnchorRenderReportTests.test_stale_tag_render_report_carries_no_timing_field (red only
    incidentally, via its own "input precondition" assertion that a flag actually landed --
    the timing-field scan itself never ran)

The 9 that stayed GREEN under total feature disablement include EVERY dedicated "does not flag"
test in the suite:
  test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_nothing
  test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_a_reformat_across_two_extractions
  test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_an_unrelated_anchor
  test_stale_tag_render_report_does_not_flag_a_reformat
  test_stale_tag_render_report_does_not_fail_the_build (trivially true when nothing is ever
    flagged, so of course the exit code stays 0)
  test_stale_tag_span_hash_is_persisted_on_every_anchored_statement (checks a different property,
    correctly orthogonal to this attack)
  SpanHashUnitTests' three tests (hash-unchanged-by-reformat, hash-unchanged-by-docstring-edit,
    hash-changes-on-real-change) -- these call span_hash() directly, a genuinely different, lower
    unit than run()'s diffing, correctly untouched by an attack on run()'s emission path, and NOT
    vacuous on their own terms: test_stale_tag_hash_changes_on_a_real_body_change already gives
    them their own internal positive control (h1 != h2 on a real mutation), so these three are
    fine as written.

This is exactly the shape the handoff named ("the same defect class as this run's tc38 and tc47")
and exactly the threshold the handoff pre-declared as BLOCK-worthy ("if most of the negatives stay
green ... that is a BLOCK-worthy finding even though the feature works"). 6 of the 9 EXTRACTION-
and RENDER-level tests in this gate's own two headline test classes (StaleAnchorExtractionTests,
StaleAnchorRenderReportTests) -- everything except the two "flags a real change" tests and the
persisted-hash test -- would not catch a regression that silently disabled staleness detection
entirely. A future refactor that accidentally comments out or short-circuits the `stale =
sorted(...)` line (or any equivalent full-disable) ships green.

The feature ITSELF genuinely works -- the two "flags" tests have real teeth (confirmed: they are
exactly what went red) -- so this is not a claim the capability is broken. It is a claim that most
of the shipped regression guard cannot fail, which CREW_CONTEXT.md's verification-discipline
section lists first among the rules that most often separate an accepted change from a reworked
one here ("A check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passed").

RULING: BLOCKING. Fix shape: give each "does not flag" test its own positive control in the SAME
test method (assert a known-should-flag mutation DOES flag, in the same test that asserts the
target case does not) -- e.g. test_stale_tag_does_not_flag_an_unrelated_anchor already builds the
fixture where widget-spin SHOULD be stale; it should also assert "widget-spin" IS in
_stale_slugs(after) in the SAME method it asserts "holder-hold" is not, so a full-disable
regression cannot leave it green. Same shape applies to test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_
nothing (add a second extraction in the same test that DOES flag) and to the two render-report

=== Q1: Does slug-match beg the question? CORRECTLY-DEFERRED G7 CONCERN, not a defect now ===

Confirmed directly: grepped scripts/code_map/ for comment-tag vocabulary (Assumption:/
Constraint:/etc.) -- zero hits, and the real repo's own fresh render_report.json (built this
review, see below) shows "ids": 0, zero anchors anywhere in this corpus today. The ONLY authored-
identity surface that exists pre-g7 is the [slug] anchor itself, so matching old-vs-new by slug
IS the only "same tag" test available today -- the crew's reasoning holds as stated.

Going further than the crew's own writeup: this mechanism tracks the CODE's hash only, never a
tag's own prose (which does not exist yet). Once g7 lands, this has a real, permanent consequence
that is NOT a bug g7 will "fix" by widening the hook -- it is baked into what span_hash measures:
the flag fires on ANY code change under a live tag, EVEN ONE where the human already updated the
tag's prose correctly in the same commit. There is no way for this mechanism, as built, to
distinguish "prose is now stale" from "prose was already fixed, but the code changed too." That
is consistent with the crew's own accepted-cost stance on the local-variable-rename blind spot
(over-flag, never under-flag, is the accepted direction of error) -- see the Decision-anchor
ruling below -- so I read this as the SAME accepted direction of error, not a new problem, but it
should be named explicitly as a permanent design property for g7 to inherit, not something g7's
build will make go away.

RULING: correctly-deferred g7 concern. No rework required now.

=== Q2: Is advisory-only right, and does the FAIL text collide? COLLISION CONFIRMED, real finding ===

Confirmed by reading checks.py directly: checks.run() (the `check` subcommand) prints REAL,
build-relevant failures as `FAIL {name}: {count}` (scripts/code_map/checks.py:833) -- the exact
same "FAIL " prefix convention render.py's new advisory line uses: `FAIL stale tag [%s]: ...`
(render.py:721). render.py ALSO already used this convention for an unambiguous, build-failing
condition: `FAIL duplicate id [%s] claimed by: %s` (render.py:713), which DOES fail the build
(`return 1 if duplicates else 0`, render.py:730) -- while the new stale-tag line, by design, never
affects the return code.

Traced the call graph via cli.py: `build` runs extract.run() then render.run() (cli.py's
_build) -- so a SINGLE `build` invocation's own stdout can legally contain BOTH "FAIL duplicate
id [...]" (build-failing) and "FAIL stale tag [...]" (advisory only) side by side, distinguishable
ONLY by exit code, never by the printed text. `check` is a SEPARATE subcommand (checks.py's own
run(), never calls render.py) -- so the two conventions never appear in the SAME command's stdout,
but they DO appear in the same combined transcript for the gate's own documented standard
procedure ("Fresh build then check (in that order)"): a human or script reading that transcript
end to end sees three different "FAIL "-prefixed line shapes across the two commands, two of which
are build-failing and one of which is not.

This is exactly what the handoff asked me to check for, and it is real: "whether anything (a
script, a CI grep, a human skimming) could reasonably read FAIL and conclude the build failed."
Yes -- the SAME prefix a real check failure already uses, in the SAME command's own output, in the
gate's own standard-procedure transcript.

Severity: I agree advisory-only is the right SEVERITY given this repo's own inherited stance (a
stale tag is not unambiguous corruption the way a duplicate id is; failing the build on it would
train people to ignore a real signal, matching the code's own "gb's ruling" comment -- I checked
this citation and could not find gb's OWN gate producing a literal ruling about build-failing vs
advisory severity specifically; gb's actual scope is the four ratio-based thresholds. The
"twitchy tripwire" language traces to this gate's own Commander plan
(g6-implementer-plan.json:185), not a verbatim gb decision. Not a blocker on its own -- the
REASONING is sound and consistent with gb's own documented philosophy of avoiding twitchy
absolute-count invariants -- but the citation is looser than "the gb ruling" implies; worth a
lighter phrasing next time ("in the spirit of gb's ratio-over-count philosophy") rather than
citing it as a specific ruling.

RULING on severity: advisory-only stands. RULING on the text collision: real, should-fix, not on
its own blocking (Q4 is what blocks this gate), but should be fixed in the same rework pass --
change the advisory line's prefix to something that cannot be mistaken for a build-failing check
(e.g. "ADVISORY stale tag [...]" or "WARN stale tag [...]"), a one-line fix.

=== Q3: Attack reformatting immunity with novel mutations -- ALL PREDICTIONS CONFIRMED, no new defect ===

Wrote a standalone attack script calling extract.span_hash() directly on 8 paired snippets NOT
in the crew's own probe set (quote-style change, backslash line continuation, paren-wrapped
multi-line, changed default-argument value, reordered independent statements, added a type
annotation, integer-literal-to-equivalent-expression, for-loop-to-comprehension), predicting
flag/no-flag BEFORE running each. Result: 8/8 predictions matched exactly.

No-flag confirmed (all three lexical-only changes): quote-style, backslash-continuation,
paren-wrap -- consistent with ast.dump encoding the Constant VALUE and node structure only, never
source text/whitespace (include_attributes=False, as the docstring already states).

Flag confirmed (all four AST-structural changes, even where runtime BEHAVIOR is unchanged):
default-arg-value, statement-reorder (ast.dump encodes body-list order), add-type-annotation
(a new AST node), int-literal-to-equivalent-expression (Constant(2) vs BinOp(1+1) differ in AST
though the runtime value is identical), for-loop-to-comprehension (very different AST shapes for
equivalent behavior).

Every result follows directly and only from ast.dump's documented behavior -- nothing accidental,
nothing that contradicts the crew's own stated mechanism. The syntactic-but-behaviorally-inert
false-positive cases (literal-to-equivalent-expression, reordering, annotations) are the SAME
accepted "over-flag, never under-flag" direction of error already named for the local-variable-
rename blind spot -- not a new defect class, but worth naming precisely: the immunity claim holds
EXACTLY as claimed (reformatting/comments/docstrings), and nothing more.

RULING: no defect. Confirms the crew's own claim precisely, with 8 novel mutations, no accidental
behavior found.

   reviewer workflow (each gate's close criteria run `build` into the SAME default `--artifacts`

   observation, not a blocker: the mechanism's only exerciser is an unenforced convention (don't

2. Read-before-overwrite robustness -- REPRODUCED A REAL CRASH, not previously reported.
   - First-ever run (no previous statements.jsonl): confirmed safe by the shipped
     test_stale_tag_first_extraction_flags_nothing (os.path.exists(outp) False -> old_hashes={}).
   - Slug newly added or removed between runs: confirmed safe by direct code read -- a new slug is
     only in new_hashes (never compared, no flag, no crash); a removed slug is only in old_hashes
     (the loop iterates new_hashes.items(), never visits it) -- matches the code's own comment
     ("this gate's concern... see DESIGN_SPEC's Tombstones section").
   - Truncated / malformed previous statements.jsonl: REPRODUCED A CRASH. Built a real fixture
     repo, ran `extract` once (succeeds), truncated the last line of the resulting
     statements.jsonl mid-JSON (simulating an interrupted prior run -- a real scenario, since
     extract.run()'s OWN writer is a plain `with open(outp, "w")` with no atomic rename, so a
     killed process leaves exactly this kind of partial last line), then ran `extract` again
     against the same --artifacts dir. Result: uncaught `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Invalid
     control character...`, propagating all the way out, exit code 1, with a bare Python
     traceback naming no file path and no actionable next step. This is a NEW failure mode this
     gate introduces: before g6, extract.run() never read the old store, so a corrupted leftover
     statements.jsonl from an earlier interrupted run was harmless (the next run would just
     overwrite it and succeed). Now a corrupted leftover store makes EVERY subsequent extraction
     fail outright until a human manually deletes the file, and the traceback gives no hint that
     THIS is the fix. Not tested anywhere in the shipped suite (grepped
     StaleAnchorExtractionTests/StaleAnchorRenderReportTests -- no malformed-store test exists).
     RULING: real robustness regression, should-fix (wrap the old-hash read in a try/except that
     treats an unreadable store as absent, printing a named warning, mirroring "fail visibly"
     doctrine -- crashing IS visible, but with no actionable message and a NEW failure mode where
     none existed before). Contributes to, but does not by itself drive, the BLOCK verdict (Q4
     already drives it).

3. Count discrepancy -- CONFIRMED: "12" is right, "16" in the RESULT's Scope section is simply
   wrong. Counted directly from the diff: StaleAnchorExtractionTests (5 methods) +
   StaleAnchorRenderReportTests (4 methods) + SpanHashUnitTests (3 methods) = 12, matching the
   Evidence section and my own independent test run (12 passed, both before and after my
   revert). Nothing was dropped between writing and shipping -- this is a drafting error confined
   to the RESULT document's Scope section, not a shipped-behavior defect.

4. extract_report.json's secondary stale_tags field -- judged: harmless duplication on the
   BLESSED `build` path (extract then render in one process, same statements.jsonl round-tripped

   extract.run() -- extract_report.json writes `stale` directly; render_report.json re-derives
   the same slugs by reading the very statements.jsonl rows that same `stale` list just produced.
   They cannot diverge within one `build` invocation. BUT the CLI supports invoking `extract` and
   `render` as independently-timed stages (cli.py's own STAGES tuple), and if a human runs `render`
   alone against a `statements.jsonl` from an OLDER `extract` run than the one that produced the

   different runs. This is not new to this gate -- extract_report.json's existing `failures` field
   carries the identical latent risk today, pre-dating g6 -- so I do not treat this as a g6-
   specific defect, just as an observation worth naming since the handoff asked directly. Filed as
   a triage candidate below (tc1), not a blocker.

The DEMONSTRATES-THE-BEHAVIOR question is where this splits:

- The NEGATIVE evidence -- the 6 "does not flag" tests offered as proof the mechanism correctly

triage_candidates.statement: tc(new): read-before-overwrite robustness gap in extract.run() (gate g6). A truncated/malformed leftover statements.jsonl from an interrupted prior extraction (extract.run()'s writer is a plain 'with open(outp, w)', no atomic rename, so a killed process leaves a partial last line) now crashes EVERY subsequent extraction with an uncaught json.decoder.JSONDecodeError and a bare traceback naming no file/line -- reproduced this review against a real fixture. Before this gate, a corrupted leftover store was harmless (the next run just overwrote it). Fix: wrap the old-hash read in a try/except that treats an unreadable/malformed previous store as absent, printing a named warning, consistent with fail-visibly-with-an-actionable-message doctrine. Evidence: .agent-work/issue-456/g6-review/review.json r1-handoff finding, Also-verify item 2.

tc(new): render.py's advisory stale-tag line prints with the literal FAIL prefix (FAIL stale tag [...]), the exact same convention checks.py uses for real, build-relevant failures (FAIL {name}: {count}) and render.py itself already uses for the build-failing duplicate-id case (FAIL duplicate id [...]). A single build invocation's own stdout can legally contain both the build-failing and the advisory-only FAIL line side by side, distinguishable only by exit code -- a script grepping FAIL, or a human skimming the gate's own documented build-then-check transcript, could reasonably misread the advisory as a real failure. Advisory-only SEVERITY is correct and not in question; only the TEXT collides. Fix: change the advisory line's prefix to something that cannot be mistaken for a build-failing check, e.g. ADVISORY stale tag [...] or WARN stale tag [...] -- a one-line change. Evidence: .agent-work/issue-456/g6-review/review.json r1-handoff finding, Q2.
